name: Tretinoin protocol (tret, buffering)
lead: The tretinoin protocol, usually shortened to "tret" on looksmaxxing forums, is the way people ease into topical tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid, sold as Retin-A, Avita, Renova and generics) and manage its irritation. Users aim for smoother, clearer, more even-toned and firmer-looking skin, with fewer visible acne marks, age spots and fine lines. Many describe starting with infrequent applications that increase as the skin adapts, and "buffering" the product with moisturiser.[1][2]

Tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied topical retinoid for photoageing.[1] A 1988 double-blind trial in JAMA found that all 30 patients who completed 16 weeks improved on tretinoin-treated forearms, and 14 of 15 improved on the face, with no improvement on vehicle-treated skin.[14] A 22-month follow-up reported that gains in wrinkling and texture were maintained when strength or frequency was reduced, and that discrete sun-spots fell by 71 percent.[14] Reviews place tretinoin as the most potent and most studied retinoid for skin ageing, with irritation the main limit on acceptance.[14][15]

Buffering itself, meaning applying moisturiser before or over the retinoid, is a community and clinician convention rather than a subject of published trials. Wikipedia's tretinoin article describes gradual introduction (every second or third night at first), waiting after washing the face, and a non-comedogenic moisturiser as management steps for irritation.[1] On forums, users also discuss eyelid use, face-slimming claims, strength and dose frequency, and combining it with other routines such as dermarolling.[3][4][5][12]

chain: Retinoid gradually introduced to the face
Skin tolerates it with less irritation and flaking
Collagen, texture and tone improve over weeks to months
angle.text: People use a slow ramp and moisturiser buffering so they can stay on tretinoin long enough to see smoother texture, fewer fine lines, more even tone and faded acne marks. Some forum users also say it leaves the face leaner.

paras: Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid, a first-generation retinoid, the class of vitamin A derivatives that act through retinoic acid and retinoid X receptors in skin cells.[1][8] Topical forms (cream, gel, lotion, microsphere gel) are used for acne and for photoaged skin. A 0.05% lotion was developed to improve tolerability, and light or oxidising agents such as benzoyl peroxide can degrade the molecule, which led to microencapsulated formulations.[1]

The "tret protocol" in appearance communities refers to the routine around the drug: starting at low frequency, raising it as the skin adapts, and layering moisturiser (buffering) to moderate dryness and peeling.[3][4] Wikipedia lists comparable steps as irritation management: beginning every other or every third night, waiting at least 20 minutes after washing and drying the face, gently exfoliating fine flaking and using a non-comedogenic moisturiser if needed.[1] Forum users ask related questions, such as whether moisturiser applied afterwards rubs the medicine off and whether applying a lower strength twice matches a higher strength once.[6][7]

Reference sources also advise sun protection, because retinoids thin the stratum corneum and can increase sun sensitivity even though they are not true photosensitisers.[1] A skin-care overview describes sunscreen and moisturiser as the standard companions of any active routine.[16]

Topical retinoids increase collagen production, thicken the epidermis and reduce abnormal pigment-cell and keratinocyte changes in photoaged skin; improvement takes weeks to months.[1] A 1996 review reported that a tretinoin emollient cream partly reversed photodamage in multicentre trials within four to six months when used with sun protection and moisturisers.[17] Tretinoin also speeds the fading of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after acne, including in darker skin.[1]

In acne, tretinoin binds retinoic acid receptors in keratinocytes, normalises follicular keratinisation, reduces microcomedones and competes with inflammatory signalling, which is why it is used both to clear breakouts and for maintenance.[1] Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists tretinoin among topical treatments studied for wrinkles.[2] Users commonly describe a first phase of flaking and apparent roughness before texture improves, though published trials describe this as a retinoid reaction that lessened over time.[14]

Common topical reactions are irritation, redness, swelling, peeling and, in some cases, blistering; users report increased sun sensitivity, attributed to a thinner stratum corneum. It should not be applied to the eyes or mucous membranes, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy because of birth-defect risk.[1] The American Academy of Dermatology is quoted as stating that retinoids should not be used during pregnancy, while topical forms are absorbed much less than oral ones.[8]

The reviewed trials describe irritation as the main side effect, and a 2006 review says burning, scaling and dermatitis limit acceptance, particularly with tretinoin and tazarotene, whereas retinaldehyde and retinol are less irritating.[14][1] On looksmax.org, one user asked about eyelid application and the risk of dry or red eyes, and another thread carries a warning for tretinoin users about meibomian glands.[3][5] Others report rashes and a very red face during use.[9]

Retinoid receptors regulate cell differentiation, and topical retinoids are thought to act on the epidermis and dermis by thickening the epidermis, boosting collagen and normalising keratinocyte turnover.[1] Topical retinoids generally do not pass through intact skin in large amounts unless the barrier is compromised.[8]

Variants discussed in appearance communities include different tretinoin strengths and vehicles (cream versus gel versus microsphere), lower-strength maintenance, and milder cosmetic precursors such as retinol and retinaldehyde, which reviews describe as less irritating but less studied.[1][14][15] Prescription alternatives such as adapalene and tazarotene belong to later generations of the class.[8]

Tretinoin is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and is available as a generic; it is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia.[1] Topical use during pregnancy is contraindicated according to the label-derived guidance summarised on Wikipedia.[1]

Tretinoin was patented in 1957 and approved for medical use in 1962. James Fulton and Albert Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania developed its use for acne in the 1960s, and the FDA approved it for acne in 1971 as Retin-A.[1][13] Early phase I trials were run on inmates at Holmesburg Prison, a context that Wikipedia's biography of Kligman describes as a textbook example of unethical experimentation and which led to later restrictions on prison research.[1][13]

Its use for photoageing later made it a mainstay of cosmetic dermatology; the 1988 JAMA trial is a landmark in that shift.[14] The FDA approved the microsphere gel (Retin-A Micro) in 1997.[1] A separate oral use for acute promyelocytic leukaemia was introduced in a 1988 clinical trial at Ruijin Hospital in Shanghai.[1] Newer retinoids include third-generation adapalene and tazarotene and, from 2019, fourth-generation trifarotene.[8]

A 16-week randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled study (Weiss and colleagues, JAMA 1988) applied tretinoin to one forearm and vehicle to the other; every completer improved on the treated forearm and 14 of 15 improved on the treated face, with histological change only in treated skin and irritation the only reported side effect.[14]

A 22-month extension (Ellis and colleagues, JAAD 1990) found that improvements were maintained even when dose or frequency was reduced, with a 71 percent fall in discrete lentigines and epidermal thickening on histology.[14] A 2006 overview of retinoids for skin ageing and a 2022 focused review both describe tretinoin as having the strongest clinical support among retinoids, with many cosmetic retinoids lacking well-designed trials.[14][15]
No published trials have tested buffering with moisturiser or slow-ramp schedules as defined in forum protocols, and no studies were found on facial fat reduction.

Retin-A is a regular topic on looksmax.org. Threads cover how long a tube lasts, low-dose long-term use, collagen concerns, and whether it affects the nose or cheek fullness.[4][10][11] Users often pair it with other skin routines such as dermarolling and, for hair, other drugs, and discuss sourcing generics from abroad, which this wiki does not detail.[12]

One user wrote after six months on tretinoin and a cutting phase that his cheek fat looked flatter and attributed it to both, while noting acne scars looked more visible at first.[4] Another long-term user said he still had forehead lines and crow's feet after years of use and called anti-ageing a "meme".[12] Such posts sit beside the clinical literature, which reports maintained improvement under continued use.[14]

timeline.event: Fulton and Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania develop its use for acne.[1][13]
JAMA double-blind trial reports improvement in photoaged skin; Shanghai trial introduces oral use for leukaemia.[14][1]
22-month follow-up reports sustained improvement with reduced dosing.[14]
Review reports partial reversal of photodamage in multicentre tretinoin trials.[17]
FDA approves the microsphere gel (Retin-A Micro).[1]
Trifarotene, a fourth-generation retinoid, is approved in the US.[8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org tretinoin is discussed as an anti-ageing, skin-quality and face-slimming tool, with threads on strength, frequency and side effects.[4][6][10]

claims.claim: Tret slims a bloated face over several months
claims.believers: One user reported that after about six months of tretinoin plus cutting, his malar fat looked flatter and others commented on hollow cheeks.[4] Other threads ask whether it burns buccal or facial fat.[10][11]
claims.experts: No published studies were found showing tretinoin reduces facial fat; reference sources describe collagen, epidermal and pigmentation effects.[1]

claims.claim: Applying near the eyes can improve eyelid skin
claims.believers: A user wanting collagen rebuilding on the eyelids asked about use there.[3]
claims.experts: Product guidance states tretinoin is not to be applied to eyes or mucous membranes.[1] Another forum thread warns about meibomian glands.[5]

claims.believers: Users discuss layering moisturiser to cushion retinoid dryness and ask whether it rubs off the medicine.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists a non-comedogenic moisturiser and gradual frequency as irritation measures, but no trials test buffering as such.[1]

claims.claim: Long-term retinoid use prevents visible ageing
claims.believers: Users take retinoids for collagen and wrinkle prevention; one long-term user was disappointed, citing persistent forehead lines.[12]
claims.experts: Studies up to two years show improvement in photoaged skin, with maintenance use possible.[1]

claims.claim: Retinoids slow visible ageing if used for years
claims.believers: Users take retinoids for collagen and wrinkle prevention and trade long-term experience reports.[12]
claims.experts: A 22-month trial extension reported maintained improvement with reduced frequency, and reviews call tretinoin the best-supported retinoid for photoageing.[14][15]

claims.claim: Tret makes acne scars look worse before they look better
claims.believers: One user noticed acne scars looking more visible in the first months on tretinoin and hoped it would eventually help fill them.[4]
claims.experts: Trials describe a retinoid reaction that lessened over time, and Wikipedia reports faster fading of post-acne dark marks; no trials on scar depth were located.[14][1]

card.summary: Slow-ramped, moisturiser-buffered prescription retinoid use; tretinoin itself is well studied, the buffering routine is not.
card.note: Prescription retinoid; contraindicated in pregnancy; causes irritation and sun sensitivity.

quick.overview:
The tret protocol is community shorthand for easing into prescription tretinoin and cushioning it with moisturiser.

Tretinoin is the most studied topical retinoid for photoageing; no studies were found on buffering specifically.
quick.mechanism: Tretinoin acts on retinoic acid receptors in skin cells, normalising follicle keratinisation and, per reports, boosting collagen. Buffering is meant to reduce irritation, not change the mechanism.
quick.risks: Irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is available by prescription in many countries.
